summary: The window contains a dense cluster of geopolitical and political shocks, culminating in the collapse of the Syrian government: rebel forces advanced from Aleppo (Day 4) through Hama (Day 10) and Homs (Day 12) to seize Damascus and the Presidential Palace, with Assad reported granted asylum in Moscow (Day 13), followed immediately by Israeli airstrikes on Syrian military and chemical/ballistic weapons sites and the appointment of a transitional prime minister (Days 13–14). Layered on top are two abrupt developed-market political ruptures — the South Korean president's declaration of martial law and ensuing impeachment proceedings (Days 8–9) and the collapse of the French government on a no-confidence vote (Day 9) — plus the annulment of a Romanian presidential election round (Day 11). Any of these could account for a regime change in volatility; together they form a plausible composite driver.
mechanism: A sudden state collapse in a Middle Eastern producer region, combined with Iranian evacuations, Israeli strikes and Turkish/Kurdish fighting, raises energy and regional-conflict risk premia, while the martial-law episode in South Korea and the fall of the French government inject direct sovereign, currency and equity risk into two significant markets — all of which widen the distribution of expected outcomes and lift realised and implied volatility.

claims.claim: Rebel forces led by Tahrir al-Sham advanced rapidly across Syria, entering Aleppo, then Hama, Salamiyah and Homs within roughly a week.
Rebel forces seized the Presidential Palace in Damascus and Russian state media reported that Bashar al-Assad and his family had been granted asylum in Moscow.
Israel struck Syrian air bases and the Damascus Scientific Research Center overseeing chemical weapons and ballistic missile programmes immediately after the regime's fall.
Iran began evacuating military personnel, diplomatic staff and civilians from Syria amid the rebel advance.

A transitional Syrian government was formed with Mohammed al-Bashir appointed prime minister on the final day of the window, while fighting continued in Manbij between Turkish-backed forces and the SDF, killing around 50.
South Korea's president declared martial law, protesters attempted to storm the National Assembly, impeachment proceedings began, and the president subsequently apologised.
The French government collapsed after 331 of 577 deputies backed a no-confidence motion.
Romania's Constitutional Court annulled the first round of the presidential election two days before the runoff.
A ceasefire in Lebanon was agreed at the start of the window but was repeatedly reported as violated by both sides.
The EU and Mercosur finalised a free trade agreement after 25 years of negotiations.

competing_explanation: The volatility flag may be driven mainly by the developed-market political shocks rather than Syria: the South Korean martial-law declaration and impeachment process (Days 8–12) and the French no-confidence collapse (Day 9) are more directly transmissible into equity, bond and FX pricing than a regime change in a country with limited direct market linkage. A third, weaker reading is that the model flagged noise — much of the window is routine elections, weather disasters and accidents, and the Syrian conflict had been escalating gradually for eleven days rather than as a single surprise.
